lessons.title: Case Study: A Strategy With 22% CAGR on Paper That Returned 4% Live

children.text: This case study is a composite, built from the pattern that shows up again and again around quant desks and prop trading floors in India, not the disclosed numbers of any specific fund or trader. The strategy, the backtest, and the live result are illustrative. The gap between them, and where exactly it comes from, is not.
The Strategy: A Smallcap Momentum Rotation

A prop trading applicant builds a rules-based rotation strategy on the Nifty Smallcap 250. Every week, the 20 stocks with the strongest 3-month price momentum are held; anything that drops out of that top group is sold and replaced. Roughly a quarter of the 20-stock book turns over in a typical week. Five years of backtested data, sourced from NSE bhavcopy archives and rebuilt in Python, shows a strategy that looks genuinely good.

stats.context: Ranked and rotated on 3-month price momentum

stats.label: Backtested CAGR
stats.context: 5-year backtest, gross of all trading costs

children.text: 22.4% CAGR against a Nifty Smallcap 250 benchmark that returned single digits over the same stretch is the kind of number that gets a strategy fast-tracked toward real capital. The backtest, like most backtests at this stage, assumed every rebalance filled at the closing price shown in the data, with no brokerage, no STT, and no consideration of whether the market could actually absorb the size being traded.

Satisfied with the backtest, the desk deploys ₹2 crore, split into 20 positions of roughly ₹10 lakh each, and runs the strategy live for a year, executing the same weekly rotation rules through a broker's order execution API. At the end of the year, the actual return in the trading account is 4.1%, not 22.4%.

body.text: As stated above, this is a composite case study constructed to illustrate a common and well-documented pattern. It is not a report of any specific fund's or trader's actual disclosed performance.

children.text: Decomposing the Gap: Where the 18.3 Points Went
The 18.3 percentage point gap between 22.4% and 4.1% is not one thing, it is three, and they hit the strategy at three different, sequential stages.

body.caption: The three components of the 18.3-point gap

cells: Transaction costs (brokerage, STT, stamp duty, exchange charges, GST)

children.text: Why Market Impact Was the Biggest Culprit

Transaction costs were the most predictable component and, at 6.8 points, the smallest. They follow directly from the Chapter 2 cost stack applied to roughly 25% weekly turnover, and the desk had already modeled them reasonably well going in. Spread slippage added 4.1 points, unsurprising given that smallcap bid-ask spreads run far wider than the 0.02% to 0.05% typical of a Nifty 50 name. Market impact, at 7.4 points, was the biggest and least anticipated hit. Each ₹10 lakh position was being sized against smallcap stocks whose average daily traded value can sit anywhere from ₹1 crore to ₹5 crore, meaning a single rebalance order could represent 2% to 10% of that day's entire volume in the name. Orders that size do not fill at the quoted price, they move it, on both the buy and the sell side, every single week.

body.text: Notice that transaction costs, the part covered in Chapter 2, were the smallest and most manageable piece of the gap. Market impact, which does not appear on any contract note and has no published rate card, did the most damage. A desk that only modeled the Chapter 2 cost stack, and stopped there, would have walked into this result with real capital and no warning. Chapter 3 exists to close exactly that blind spot.

children.text: What Would Have Caught This Before Going Live

Three checks would have surfaced this gap before a single rupee of real capital was risked. First, model transaction costs with the full Chapter 2 cost stack, not a rough guess. Second, model spread and market impact using average daily traded value for the actual universe being traded, not the more liquid large-cap names the strategy's rules happen to be tested on paper against. Third, size the backtest at the intended live capital, ₹2 crore and ₹10 lakh per position here, not at whatever notional size makes the historical data easiest to work with. A strategy that looks identical at ₹2 lakh and ₹2 crore in a backtest is usually a sign the backtest is not accounting for size at all.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: In this case study, which single component accounted for the largest share of the gap between the 22.4% backtest and the 4.1% live result?
options: Transaction costs (brokerage, STT, stamp duty, exchange charges, GST)
body.explanation: Market impact accounted for 7.4 of the 18.3 points lost, about 40% of the total gap, more than transaction costs and spread slippage combined at roughly 60%. It was the largest single component precisely because it was the one component the desk had not modeled before going live.

body.text: A 22% backtest becoming a 4% live result is not one failure, it is three stacked on top of each other: transaction costs, spread slippage, and market impact, hitting in that order as capital moves from a spreadsheet into a real order book. The component with no published rate card, market impact, is often the one that does the most damage.

points: The gap between backtested and live returns is rarely one cost, it typically decomposes into transaction costs, spread slippage, and market impact, each hitting the strategy at a different stage.
In this case study, transaction costs were the smallest and most predictable component, while market impact, driven by position size relative to average daily traded value, was the largest.

Smallcap and midcap strategies are especially exposed to market impact because average daily traded value is far lower than in large caps, so the same rupee position size represents a much bigger share of daily volume.
A backtest should be sized and tested at the capital the strategy will actually trade with, since costs and impact that are invisible at a small notional size can dominate the result at real size.
